title: Google Business Profile Suspended: Why It Happens and How to Get It Back
excerpt: Why Google suspends Business Profiles, how to fix the cause and appeal, and what to avoid while you wait. Written for UK and Irish businesses.
content:
If your Google Business Profile is suspended, Google has decided the profile breaks its guidelines, and you get it back by fixing the cause and sending one appeal through the Google Business Profile appeals tool, with documents that show your business name and address. Do not create a new profile for the same business while you wait: Google's own help pages tell you not to. In the UK and Ireland the appeals tool also handles rejected edits and media restrictions, and Google says a review can take up to five working days.

What does a suspended Google Business Profile mean?

Google may suspend or disable profiles that do not follow its guidelines for representing your business on Google. When a profile is removed, the public cannot see it, and owners and managers cannot act on it. The appeals tool shows the reason and the policy Google says you broke.

People in the local search industry talk about two levels. BrightLocal suggests a simple test: search for your business on Google Maps. If the listing has gone, that is a hard suspension, and the listing can lose its reviews. If it still shows but you can no longer manage it, that is a soft suspension, which is usually tied to the Google Account that manages it.

Google also separates the profile from the people behind it. If the owner's Google Account is removed, every location that person owns is removed with it. If only a manager's account is removed, that manager loses access, but the locations stay. So before you change anything on the profile, check which account the problem sits with.

Why do Google Business Profiles get suspended?

The reason Google gives can be short, so compare your profile with the rules behind the most common suspensions. These come from Google's guidelines, with the ones that matter most for UK and Irish trades and small businesses.

Extra words in the business name

The name has to be the name you use in the real world, on your van, your signage, your invoices and your website. Google lists what is not allowed, including taglines, service or product information, location information, phone numbers and words in capitals. Its guidelines say unnecessary information in the name could result in the suspension of your profile. "Smith Plumbing" is fine if that is your trading name; "Smith Plumbing Emergency Plumber Leeds 24/7" is the kind of name the guidelines rule out. Legal terms such as Ltd are only allowed when your signage or invoices consistently use them.

An address you do not work from

A business that rents a mailing address but does not operate from it is not eligible for a Business Profile, and P.O. boxes are not accepted. A desk in a co-working space only counts if it has clear signage, receives customers during your hours and is staffed by your own staff during those hours.

A home address on show for a service-area business

Most tradespeople go to the customer. Google calls this a service-area business and uses plumbers and cleaning services as its examples. If you do not serve customers at your address, Google says to remove the address from the profile and set service areas instead. A plumber working from home who shows the home address breaks the guidelines.

Service areas have their own rules: up to 20 areas, set by towns, cities or postcodes, not as a radius, and the whole area normally no more than about 2 hours' drive from your base. A Cork electrician listing every county in Ireland, or a Manchester roofer listing towns across England, goes well beyond that guideline.

More than one profile for the same business

Google allows only one profile per business, and its guidelines say not to create more than one page for each location, in one account or several. Google also tells you not to create a new profile for the same business after a suspension, and a second profile would break the one profile per business rule.

Phone numbers, categories and hours that do not match reality

The phone number must be under your direct control and must not redirect people to another business or a social media page. Premium-rate numbers are not accepted. Categories need to describe what the business is, using as few as possible, not keywords you would like to rank for. Hours are your real customer-facing hours: BrightLocal lists "Open 24 hours" without staff as a common trigger, and Google says businesses that work only by appointment do not give hours at all.

Lots of edits at once

BrightLocal also lists rapid repeated edits, a change from a storefront to a service-area business, and a change of address as triggers, and suggests waiting 60 seconds between edits. If you need to fix several things, make the changes calmly and check each one, rather than rewriting the whole profile in one sitting.

How do you get a suspended Google Business Profile back?

You can only appeal once for each decision, so prepare everything before you open the tool.

Step 1: Fix the cause first

Read the reason the appeals tool shows, open the linked policy and correct the profile so it follows the guidelines. Remove the extra words from the name, hide the home address and set service areas, or delete the duplicate profile. Google's first point before any appeal is to make sure the profile follows all the guidelines.

Step 2: Gather your evidence

Google lists official business registration, a business licence, tax certificates and utility bills (electricity, phone, water, internet) as examples. The business name and address on every document must match the profile you are appealing. For a sole trader, that means documents in the trading name at the address on the profile.

Step 3: Send the appeal

  1. Open the Google Business Profile appeals tool (Google links it from the Fix suspended or disabled profiles page).
  2. If you are signed in to the Google Account that manages the profile, select Confirm; otherwise select Switch account.
  3. Select the Business Profile, then Continue.
  4. Select the decision you want to appeal, then Continue. The tool shows the date, the reason, the policy and whether it can be appealed.
  5. Upload your evidence with Choose file and explain in the text box why the profile follows the guidelines. Keep it short and factual.
  6. Tick the box to confirm that all evidence is attached, then select Submit appeal.

Two practical warnings that are easy to miss. First, BrightLocal reports that you have 60 minutes to upload evidence once you continue, so have the files ready in one folder before you start. Second, Google calls the evidence optional, but it lists examples of the documents to send, so include them. BrightLocal adds that the explanation box takes up to 1,000 characters and to zip the files when you send more than two.

Step 4: Wait and check the status

Google says appeal reviews can take up to five working days and asks you not to send several appeals for the same issue before a decision. The status in the appeals tool shows Submitted, Approved, Not approved, Can't be appealed or Eligible for appeal, and Google emails you the decision.

What if your Google account is restricted?

Sometimes the problem is the account, not the profile. A policy violation can restrict your Google Account, which suspends every profile you manage and stops you creating or claiming new ones. In that case Google says to appeal the restriction first on the My accounts page, and only then appeal the profile.

The same logic applies to people you have added. Google states that a removed manager account only affects that manager's access, but a removed owner account takes all of the owner's locations with it. If someone who no longer works with you is still the owner, sort out ownership once the profile is back.

What if the appeal is turned down?

If Google denies the reinstatement request, you can ask for an additional review through the local appeals contact form. Google asks for evidence you did not send with the first appeal, such as a newer utility bill or a tax certificate you left out the first time.

Businesses in the European Economic Area, which includes Ireland, have one more option under the EU Digital Services Act: Google says you can refer the appeal to an out-of-court dispute settlement body. UK businesses use the same appeals tool as the EEA for suspensions, rejected edits and media restrictions, but that out-of-court option is listed for the EEA only.

What should you avoid after a suspension?

  • Do not create a new profile. Google says this in both of its appeal help pages.
  • Do not send the same appeal twice. Wait for the decision.
  • Do not edit the name, address or category while a verification postcard is on its way. Google's verification guide warns that editing these while you wait for the code stops the code working. If a "Get verified" button appears on your profile again, Google could not fully verify the business, so verify again.
  • Do not share your verification code. Google will never ask for it. Do not give it to anyone, including people who help manage your profile.
  • Do not rely on the profile alone. The public cannot see a removed profile, so your own website is where customers can still find your phone number and details while you wait.

How can you stop it happening again?

Several of the causes above are details set at the start: a name with keywords, a home address on show, or a second profile someone made years ago.
